overviewHtml:
This ungraded knowledge check assesses your understanding of how a pretrained model is turned into an assistant. You'll be asked about fine-tuning, training with human feedback, published behavior guidelines, system instructions and safety training, and open-weight and closed models.

Note: Use this to test yourself, review the feedback on any questions you miss, and retry until you feel confident before moving forward.

forms.stemHtml: A developer takes a base model and trains it further on several thousand examples of requests paired with good replies. What is this step most likely to change?

options.html: The date of the model's knowledge cutoff
options.text: The date of the model's knowledge cutoff
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Further training on a few thousand conversations doesn't move the cutoff or add broad knowledge. Fine-tuning mainly changes how the model responds: its format, its manner, and whether it carries out instructions.

options.html: The amount of text the model can take in at once
options.text: The amount of text the model can take in at once
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. That is the context window, which fine-tuning doesn't set. Fine-tuning mainly changes how the model responds: its format, its manner, and whether it carries out instructions.

options.html: How the model responds to a request
options.text: How the model responds to a request
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! Fine-tuning on demonstrations shifts format, manner, and instruction following. The model's broad knowledge was set in its main training.

options.html: How much the model knows about world history
options.text: How much the model knows about world history
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. A few thousand examples are a tiny amount of text next to the main training collection. Fine-tuning mainly changes how the model responds: its format, its manner, and whether it carries out instructions.

forms.stemHtml: In training with human feedback, what is the reward?

options.html: A number saying how good an output is judged to be
options.text: A number saying how good an output is judged to be
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! The reward is the score an output receives. It usually comes from a second model trained to predict which replies raters would prefer.

options.html: A payment made to raters for each reply they compare
options.text: A payment made to raters for each reply they compare
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Raters are usually paid, but that isn't what the term means. The reward is a number saying how good an output is judged to be, and the model is adjusted toward outputs that score higher.

options.html: A written reply that a rater supplies as a model answer
options.text: A written reply that a rater supplies as a model answer
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. That describes demonstration data. The reward is a number saying how good an output is judged to be, and the model is adjusted toward outputs that score higher.

options.html: A setting that controls how varied the model's replies are
options.text: A setting that controls how varied the model's replies are
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. That describes temperature. The reward is a number saying how good an output is judged to be, and the model is adjusted toward outputs that score higher.

forms.stemHtml: A company publishes a document describing how it intends its AI model to behave. What is the document good evidence of?

options.html: How the model behaves in every conversation
options.text: How the model behaves in every conversation
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. The companies themselves say their models don't always match these documents. A published guideline is evidence of what the company says it's aiming for, and behavior has to be established by testing.

options.html: What text the model was trained on
options.text: What text the model was trained on
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. These documents describe intended behavior and say little about training text. A published guideline is evidence of what the company says it's aiming for.

options.html: What instructions a business has added in its own app
options.text: What instructions a business has added in its own app
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. A deploying business's instructions are usually private and aren't in the developer's document. A published guideline is evidence of what the company says it's aiming for.

options.html: What the company says it is aiming for
options.text: What the company says it is aiming for
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! These documents show stated intent. Each of the three companies discussed acknowledges that its models don't always behave as its document describes.

forms.stemHtml: The same model powers a general-purpose chatbot and a retailer's shopping assistant. The shopping assistant won't discuss anything except orders and products. What most likely accounts for the difference?

options.html: The retailer retrained the model's parameters on its catalog
options.text: The retailer retrained the model's parameters on its catalog
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. That's possible in principle, but the scenario says the model is the same. The likeliest cause is the retailer's system instructions, which are text placed ahead of the conversation and leave the parameters unchanged.

options.html: The retailer's system instructions limit the topics
options.text: The retailer's system instructions limit the topics
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! A deploying business writes system instructions that set the assistant's role and topics. They change the text in front of the model and leave its parameters as they were.

options.html: The shopping assistant has an earlier knowledge cutoff
options.text: The shopping assistant has an earlier knowledge cutoff
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. The model is the same in both products, so its cutoff is too. The likeliest cause is the retailer's system instructions, which set the assistant's topics.

options.html: The shopping assistant samples its tokens at a lower temperature
options.text: The shopping assistant samples its tokens at a lower temperature
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Temperature affects how varied replies are and wouldn't restrict topics. The likeliest cause is the retailer's system instructions, which set the assistant's topics.

forms.stemHtml: A developer publishes the parameters of one of its models for anyone to download. Which of these can a person who downloads them do? (Select all that apply.)

options.html: Run the model on their own computers
options.text: Run the model on their own computers
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! This is local deployment. Whoever holds the parameters can run the model, given suitable hardware.

options.html: Train the model further on their own examples
options.text: Train the model further on their own examples
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! The holder can fine-tune the model, which includes training away its safety behavior.

options.html: Read the full text the model was trained on
options.text: Read the full text the model was trained on
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Parameters don't contain a readable copy of the training text, and most open-weight releases don't include detailed information about the training data.

options.html: Write its instructions with none from the developer in front
options.text: Write its instructions with none from the developer in front
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! With a closed model the developer can place its own instructions ahead of every conversation. A holder of the parameters writes all the instructions.

options.html: Have the developer recall every copy if a problem emerges
options.text: Have the developer recall every copy if a problem emerges
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Published parameters can't be recalled. Copies stay wherever they have been saved.

title: From pretrained model to assistant
